title: You Know Who Really Hates AI? Insurance Claims Adjusters
gist: Glassdoor research finds insurance claims adjusters criticize AI 98 percent of the time they mention it — the most anti-AI occupation in the US workforce — as sector employment fell 21 percent between May 2025 and May 2026 and entry-level postings dropped 50 percent since 2025, with Lemonade's AI handling 96 percent of initial reports and roughly 55 percent of all claims.

themes.theme: Claims adjusting as the first visible AI displacement

insights.claim: Glassdoor research found claims adjusters who mention AI in reviews are critical 98 percent of the time, making them the most anti-AI occupation in the American workforce.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Near-unanimous worker hostility in one occupation is a usable leading indicator of where AI substitution is actually biting versus where it is still rhetoric.
insights.quote: recent research from Glassdoor found that claims adjusters who mention AI in their posts are critical a whopping 98 percent of the time

insights.claim: Employment in the claims adjusting sector dropped 21 percent between May 2025 and May 2026 according to BLS data, far faster than the BLS's own 2024 forecast of a 5 percent decline of 18,900 jobs over a full decade.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Actual displacement is running roughly an order of magnitude faster than official projections — a template for how much other AI-exposed occupation forecasts may be understating.
insights.locator: In 2024, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported

insights.claim: Entry-level claims adjuster postings have fallen 50 percent since 2025 according to Glassdoor, a sharper decline than the overall sector.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: AI is eating the bottom rung first, which destroys the training pipeline for the senior judgment roles insurers still say they need — a delayed structural cost.
insights.quote: Entry-level postings have fallen 50 percent since 2025, according to Glassdoor.

insights.claim: The BLS explicitly cited technology as a major force behind the decline in claims adjuster employment, making this one of the few occupations where the official statistical agency attributes job losses to automation.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Official attribution matters for policy — it is the kind of finding that seeds legislative attention to AI-driven displacement.
insights.locator: The BLS cited technology as a major force

insights.claim: A Glassdoor senior economist says worker reviews become increasingly anti-AI when layoffs are sensed, and when workers feel a subpar product is being forced on them or on clients — meaning sentiment data tracks both job insecurity and product quality.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Employee review sentiment is a two-signal instrument: it flags impending headcount cuts and flags AI deployments that are failing in production.
insights.quote: There's no jobs, there's no good job prospects

themes.theme: Automation depth at the leading edge

insights.claim: Lemonade's proprietary chatbot AI Jim handled initial reports 96 percent of the time by the end of last year, with automation handling roughly 55 percent of all claims.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: A disclosed 55 percent end-to-end claims automation rate is the current benchmark for what an AI-native insurer can achieve — the yardstick for every incumbent's automation claims.

insights.claim: AI startups including Liberate and Pace have raised millions on promises to reinvent insurance while incumbent insurers scale their own AI to handle more claims, creating pressure from both new entrants and internal automation.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Capital is flowing into insurance-specific AI tooling, so the displacement trend is funded and likely to accelerate regardless of worker sentiment.

insights.claim: The automated claims stack spans chatbot intake, photo and video damage estimation replacing physical inspection, AI summarization of hundreds of pages of medical records, and same-second payouts from uploaded documentation.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Each layer removes a distinct labor category — intake staff, field inspectors, medical reviewers — so the addressable cost reduction is much larger than the adjuster headcount alone.

insights.claim: Lemonade's own spokesperson concedes AI will impact many jobs and threaten many incumbents in insurance and the wider economy, and says the Glassdoor findings should be taken seriously across the industry.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The most automated player publicly acknowledging displacement removes the plausible deniability incumbents have used — relevant to how quickly disclosure and regulation follow.
insights.quote: AI is going to impact many jobs and threaten many incumbents in insurance and the economy

themes.theme: Hidden costs: hallucination, rework, and blame transfer

insights.claim: An adjuster at a major insurer describes AI-driven loss reporting producing an influx of misclassified claims that had to be rerouted, plus hallucinations in claims summaries that he unknowingly relayed to claimants and attorneys.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Automation that shifts work from removal to rework destroys the projected savings — the productivity case depends on classification accuracy nobody is auditing publicly.
insights.quote: And it's implementing more work onto the adjusters.
insights.locator: Instead, Jackson says, he and other adjusters

insights.claim: Small input defects propagate into financial errors: a smudge in an attorney's document or a missing point in an AI summary of a medical report can produce a hallucination that leads to an incorrect payout.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Incorrect payouts are a direct loss-ratio and regulatory-complaint risk, meaning AI claims automation carries a measurable downside that offsets the labor savings.

insights.claim: Customers do not realize AI is the root cause of confusion or misinformation and instead blame the human adjuster, so error costs land as reputational damage on employees rather than on the system.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Misattributed blame hides AI failure rates from management dashboards, which means internal ROI numbers for these deployments are likely overstated.

insights.claim: The article reports adjusters quitting over AI implementation rather than merely complaining, with one moving to a different carrier after the hallucination episodes.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Attrition among experienced adjusters raises the cost of the human backstop that automated systems still depend on for complex claims.

themes.theme: The limits of removing humans from loss events

insights.claim: Adjusters draw a line between AI as a tool and AI as a decision maker, with one Alabama claims executive saying it should never be given the keys.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The tool-versus-decider distinction is where regulation will eventually land in claims, so vendors selling full autonomy carry more compliance risk than copilot vendors.
insights.quote: It should never be given the keys.

insights.claim: The article's central argument is that claims handling is an emotional service delivered at a customer's worst moment, and that replacing the human with photo-based AI estimation is characterized by an experienced adjuster who lost his own home as a dangerous strategy.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Customer-experience backlash at catastrophe moments is the most likely brake on full claims automation — and a differentiation opening for carriers that keep humans in the loop.
insights.quote: AI can be helpful, but not when it’s used as a replacement for humanity.
insights.locator: I needed somebody to make sure that I'm OK

insights.claim: Traditional carriers are positioning differently from AI-natives, with State Farm emphasizing that claims require a mix of human and digital expertise and framing AI as tools that free staff to spend more time helping customers.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: A visible strategic split between AI-native and hybrid carriers means the industry will produce a natural experiment on whether full automation improves or erodes retention.
insights.locator: While more traditional insurance companies like State Farm

insights.claim: Adjusters do accept AI for low-stakes administrative work such as extending a rental car booking, indicating the resistance is task-specific rather than blanket technophobia.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Adoption succeeds in the nuisance-task tier and fails in the judgment tier — a segmentation that should guide which insurance AI vendors actually retain customers.
